name: Pale Quaker Drab
lede: Pale Quaker Drab is a muted taupe-grey, the pale tone Robert Ridgway charted beside the parent color Quaker Drab in his 1912 color atlas.

sections.title: A pale tone of Quaker Drab
sections.body:
Pale Quaker Drab puts Ridgway's tone word Pale in front of [[pebble-grey]], the paired-tone method his 1912 *Color Standards and Color Nomenclature* used across the atlas [1]. Quaker Drab itself is Ridgway's plate LI, hue 1 quintuple-prime, later filed by the ISCC-NBS dictionary of 1955 in block 265, and Maerz and Paul's 1930 *Dictionary of Color* lists it as first recorded in 1802, the oldest record of any tone in this family [1]. The name nods to the plain grey-brown dress of Quaker dress reform, though Ridgway's dictionary does not spell that out itself [1].

Its nearest named neighbor is [[bluish-grey]], 2.7 units off and close enough on screen to read as the same color [1]; [[light-mouse-grey]] sits 3.1 units away [1].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
Our archive finds this color in 917 of 23,781 paintings, 3.86 percent, as photographed; narrowing to at least five percent coverage inside a painting leaves 593 [2]. That makes it more common than 85 percent of the named colors in our library [2]. It peaks in the 1900s, present in 4.8 percent of the 1,674 paintings from that century, 1.7 times the archive's overall rate [2]. Inside a painting it most often plays a light, in 49 percent of its 593 appearances by lightness rank [2].

The earliest match dates to 1164, a floor and not a first since the archive's early centuries are thin; that is 748 years before the name's 1912 record, so the match marks a look-alike hue in an aged photograph, not a surviving pigment [2]. Arnoud van Halen used it most, in 6 of his 50 paintings here, 4.6 times the rate of the museums those works come from, and it is most over-represented in paintings from Norway, 2.3 times the expected rate [2].
